related_questions.question: Is thalassemia curable or not?
related_questions.snippet: Stem cell or bone marrow transplants are the only cure for thalassaemia, but they're not done very often because of the significant risks involved. Stem cells are produced in bone marrow, the spongy tissue found in the centre of some bones, and have the ability to develop into different types of blood cells.

related_questions.question: What does thalassemia do to a person?
related_questions.snippet: Often, thalassemia happens along with the destruction of a large number of red blood cells. This causes the spleen to get bigger and work harder than usual. An enlarged spleen can make anemia worse. It also can reduce the life of red blood cells received in a transfusion.

related_questions.question: What is the main cause of thalassemia?
related_questions.snippet: Thalassemia develops when faulty genes prevent your body from making the right amount of alpha globin or beta globin chains. When this happens, red blood cells cannot carry enough oxygen to your body's organs and tissues.

related_questions.question: Can people with thalassemia run?
related_questions.snippet: Exercise is part of an overall healthy lifestyle and helps lead to better health outcomes. Although some people with thalassemia may have trouble participating in vigorous forms of exercise, many people with thalassemia can participate in moderate physical activities including biking, running, and walking.

text_blocks.snippet: Thalassemia is a genetic blood disorder where the body doesn't produce enough hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. This leads to anemia and various other complications, with the severity depending on the type and form of thalassemia.
snippet_highlighted_words: a genetic blood disorder where the body doesn't produce enough hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen

list.title: Inherited:
list.snippet: Thalassemia is passed down through families.

list.title: Hemoglobin Deficiency:
list.snippet: The disorder affects the production of hemoglobin, leading to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of red blood cells.

list.title: Anemia:
list.snippet: Reduced hemoglobin results in anemia, causing symptoms like fatigue, weakness, and pale skin.

list.title: Types:
list.snippet: Two main types are alpha and beta thalassemia, with varying severity levels.

list.title: Severity:
list.snippet: Thalassemia can range from mild (thalassemia minor/trait) to severe (thalassemia major/Cooley's anemia).

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Symptoms can include fatigue, pale skin, slow growth, bone problems, enlarged spleen, and heart issues.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment varies depending on severity and may include blood transfusions, iron chelation therapy, and in some cases, bone marrow transplantation.

text_blocks.snippet: Thalassemia is a group of inherited blood disorders where the body makes less hemoglobin than normal. Hemoglobin is crucial for carrying oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. When hemoglobin production is impaired, red blood cells become deficient in oxygen and cannot function properly, leading to anemia and various other complications.

list.title: Alpha Thalassemia:
list.snippet: Caused by a deficiency in alpha globin chains, the protein building blocks of hemoglobin. A severe form, alpha thalassemia major (also known as Hb Bart hydrops fetalis syndrome), can be fatal before or shortly after birth.

list.title: Beta Thalassemia:
list.snippet: Caused by a deficiency in beta globin chains. Beta thalassemia major (also called Cooley's anemia) is a severe form requiring lifelong blood transfusions.

list.title: Thalassemia Minor/Trait:
list.snippet: Refers to having one copy of the gene for thalassemia, usually causing no or mild symptoms.

text_blocks.snippet: Symptoms vary depending on the type and severity of thalassemia. Common symptoms include:

list.snippet: Anemia: Fatigue, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath.
Slowed Growth: In children, anemia can affect growth and development.
Bone Problems: Expansion of bone marrow can lead to bone pain, fractures, and skeletal abnormalities.
Enlarged Spleen: The spleen may enlarge as it tries to compensate for the lack of healthy red blood cells.
Heart Problems: Severe thalassemia can lead to heart failure and irregular heart rhythms.

text_blocks.snippet: Treatment options vary depending on the severity of the condition and may include:

list.snippet: Blood Transfusions: Regular blood transfusions can help replenish healthy red blood cells and improve oxygen levels.
Iron Chelation Therapy: Excess iron can build up in the body due to frequent transfusions. Chelation therapy removes excess iron.
Bone Marrow Transplant: In severe cases, bone marrow transplantation can be a curative option.
